connections.observation: The density of ἀδικεῖν/ἀδικεῖσθαι forms (`s001`) is held in tension by the ἄκων/ἑκών contrast (`s013`): all practitioners of justice are said to practice it unwillingly (ἄκοντες), and no one is willingly just (οὐδεὶς ἑκὼν δίκαιος). Held together, these configurations make visible that the recurrent pairing of active and passive injustice is not a neutral opposition but a coerced equilibrium—the multiplication of ἀδικεῖν across the section articulates what agents would choose if capacity permitted.

The δοκεῖν/εἶναι inversion (`s002`) is enacted through the two citations of Aeschylus (`s018`): the phrase 'not to seem but to be good' is first assigned to the just man, then redirected (πολὺ ἦν ἄρα ὀρθότερον) as properly describing the unjust man who does not wish to seem but to be unjust. The reversal makes visible that the appearance/reality contrast is not a stable distinction but a transferable configuration whose assignment determines the structure of each life.

The descent into the chasm and return (καταβῆναι/ἐκβῆναι, `s004`) is answered by the completed political sequence (`s011`): becoming a messenger, seducing the queen, killing the king, seizing power. The spatial descent-and-exit frames an ascent from shepherd to ruler; held together, the two movements make visible a vertical inversion carried by the ring—what comes up from below grants the capacity to move upward in the social order.

The visibility toggle (ἀφανής/φανερός, ἄδηλος/δῆλος, `s005`) is precisely correlated with the inward/outward spatial orientation of the ring's bezel (`s006`). Held together, they make visible that appearance and spatial direction are mechanically linked: turning inward produces invisibility, turning outward produces visibility. The repeated testing (ἀποπειρᾶσθαι) of this correlation shows the power as a reproducible spatial-phenomenal operation rather than a singular event.

The δύναμις family (`s007`) moves from Glaucon's question about the δύναμις of justice itself through the inability (ἀδυναμία) grounding the social contract to the specific δύναμις granted by the ring, while the βούλομαι recurrence (`s015`) moves from Glaucon's wanting to hear a specific account to the ring-bearer's capacity to do whatever he wants (ὅτι ἂν βούληται). Held together, these trajectories make visible that the section pivots from asking what justice can do to specifying what unconstrained wanting would do—the question of power is answered by unlimited wish.

The pastoral cluster (`s010`) situates the ancestor as shepherd (ποιμήν) tending flocks before the political sequence (`s011`) transforms him into messenger, adulterer, regicide, and ruler. Held together, the configurations make visible a displacement from herding animals to political mastery, with the ring mediating the transition from one domain to another.

The sequence of tortures inflicted on the just man (`s003`)—whipping, racking, binding, eye-burning, impalement—is preceded by the purgative actions applied to him (`s016`): stripping (γυμνωτέος), testing (βεβασανισμένος), cleaning (ἐκκαθαίρεις). Held together, they make visible that the construction of the perfectly just man requires both removal and addition: external goods are stripped away, and external evils are heaped on. The βασανίζω/βεβασανισμένος echo connects judicial torture to philosophical testing.

The δοκεῖν/εἶναι contrast (`s002`) recurs across both lives while ἐπιτηδεύω (`s012`) marks the practice of each: those who practice (ἐπιτηδεύοντες) justice do so unwillingly, each is to be perfected in his own pursuit (ἐπιτήδευμα), and the unjust man practices (ἐπιτηδεύοντα) something that holds to truth. Held together, these make visible that the appearance/reality split operates differently for each practice—the just man must be real without seeming, the unjust man must seem without being, yet both are described as pursuing something, making the status of what is practiced itself uncertain.

Thrasymachus charmed like a snake (ὥσπερ ὄφις, `s014`) at the section's opening is answered by the two men cleaned like statues (ὥσπερ ἀνδριάντα, `s014`) for judgment at its close, while the just man is stripped, tested, and cleaned (`s016`). Held together, the similes make visible a movement from animate enchantment to inanimate preparation—speech that charms living resistance gives way to the purification of static figures for comparison.

The repeated αὐτὸ καθʼ αὑτό (`s008`) frames Glaucon's demand to hear justice praised in itself, while ἀκούω (`s023`) saturates the opening exchange with forms of hearing. Held together, they make visible that the isolation of justice 'itself by itself' is first an acoustic demand—Glaucon has heard many accounts but not the one he wants (ὡς βούλομαι), and the subsequent demonstration responds to a specific configuration of listening and desire rather than to a neutral question.

The κρίσις/κρίνω recurrence (`s017`) names the judgment of the two lives, while justice is placed μεταξύ and ἐν μέσῳ (`s021`) between unpunished injustice and unavenged suffering. Held together, they make visible that judgment requires spatial separation—the middle position of justice in the origin account becomes the basis for extracting two extremes that can then be judged. The judgment itself depends on a prior configuration that places justice between two other states.

Thrasymachus is charmed (κηληθῆναι, `s009`) while the perfectly unjust man is equipped to persuade (πείθειν) and use force (βιάσασθαι), and Glaucon opens with dense repetitions of ἀκούω (`s023`). Held together, these make visible a displacement of verbal compulsion: the snake-charming applied to Thrasymachus reappears as a dual capacity (persuasion and force) belonging to the unjust man, framed within Glaucon's demand to hear something he has not yet heard. The section stages listening, charming, and persuasion as linked modes of compulsion.

The unjust man's cultic advantages (`s019`)—sacrifices, dedications, service to the gods, and being more θεοφιλής—follow the ring-bearer's characterisation as ἰσόθεος (`s022`). Held together, they make visible an ironic trajectory: the power that makes one equal to a god among humans is deployed to secure divine favour, so that god-like capacity in the human realm becomes the means to win the gods' friendship. The singleton ἰσόθεος makes the cultic cluster's final claim (θεοφιλέστερον) newly visible as a reversal—godlikeness serves to court the gods.

The saturation of ἀδικέω forms (`s001`), the δύναμις/ἀδυναμία trajectory (`s007`), and the βούλομαι repetitions (`s015`) together make visible the section's governing configuration: injustice is repeatedly named as both action and suffering, capacity and incapacity determine the origin of justice, and wanting structures both Glaucon's demand and the ring's grant. Held together, these three recurrences show that the section organises itself around the conjunction of doing, being able, and wanting—justice emerges where capacity fails to meet desire.

The announced three-part structure (πρῶτον/δεύτερον/τρίτον, `s020`) organises the argument, yet the torture sequence (`s003`) that closes the just man's fate is itself a numbered sequence of five escalating actions. Held together, the two sequences make visible that the tripartite rhetorical programme gives way to a more detailed enumeration when depicting suffering—the structure promised at the outset does not govern the final intensification.

elements.context: οὐδὲν ἂν διάφορον τοῦ ἑτέρου ποιοῖ, ἀλλʼ ἐπὶ ταὔτʼ ἂν ἴοιεν ἀμφότεροι
ἵνα ἀμφότεροι εἰς τὸ ἔσχατον ἐληλυθότες

new_signals.observation: ἀμφότεροι appears at the conclusion of the ring experiment (both just and unjust would act identically if given the ring) and again at the framing of the two lives for judgment (both brought to the extreme of their respective conditions). The recurrence marks two moments where the two figures are held together for comparison.

elements.context: ἀλλὰ τέλεον ἑκάτερον εἰς τὸ ἑαυτοῦ ἐπιτήδευμα τιθῶμεν
εἰ μέλλει σφόδρα ἄδικος εἶναι. τὸν ἁλισκόμενον δὲ φαῦλον ἡγητέον· ἐσχάτη γὰρ ἀδικία
δοτέον οὖν τῷ τελέως ἀδίκῳ τὴν τελεωτάτην ἀδικίαν

new_signals.observation: Forms of τέλεος mark the perfection of each life (τέλεον ἑκάτερον, τελέως ἄδικος, τελεωτάτην ἀδικίαν), while τελευτῶν appears at the culmination of the just man's sufferings before impalement. Completion, perfection, and final extremity are lexically linked.

elements.context: ἐὰν ἄρα πῃ σφαλῇ, ἱκανὸς ἐπανορθοῦσθαι
καὶ ἐὰν ἄρα σφάλληταί τι, ἐπανορθοῦσθαι δυνατῷ εἶναι

new_signals.observation: σφάλλω appears twice in the description of the perfectly unjust man, both times paired with ἐπανορθοῦσθαι: if he stumbles in any way, he is capable of correcting the error. The capacity for self-correction is specified as part of complete injustice.

elements.context: τολμήσειεν ἀπέχεσθαι τῶν ἀλλοτρίων καὶ μὴ ἅπτεσθαι
μηδέν ποτε ἐθέλοι ἀδικῆσαι μηδὲ ἅψαιτο τῶν ἀλλοτρίων

new_signals.observation: τὰ ἀλλότρια (others' property) recurs twice in the ring scenario, both times with verbs of refraining (ἀπέχεσθαι, μὴ ἅπτεσθαι). The repetition marks what the ring-bearer could take but chooses not to, making abstention from others' goods the test case for voluntary justice.

elements.context: διὰ τὴν πλεονεξίαν, ὃ πᾶσα φύσις διώκειν πέφυκεν ὡς ἀγαθόν

new_signals.observation: πλεονεξία is named as what every nature pursues as good in the ring argument, then πλεονεκτέω recurs twice in the final enumeration of the unjust man's advantages (gaining more than enemies, gaining more and thus becoming wealthy). The noun names the universal motive; the verbs specify its successful exercise.

φίλοι and ἐχθροί appear in the description of the perfectly unjust man: he has a supply of friends and wealth to deploy force, and he benefits friends and harms enemies. The pairing articulates a traditional ethical configuration as an advantage of injustice.
